what: Run Git through its shortest alias.
when: Any time you would otherwise type git.
why: It keeps longer Git commands compact.

when: When a change is ready for the next commit.
why: It stages only the paths you name.

what: Stage every tracked and untracked change.
when: When the entire working tree belongs in one commit.
why: It captures additions, modifications, and deletions together.

when: When a file contains more than one logical change.
why: It keeps commits focused without editing files again.

what: Unstage paths while preserving their working-tree changes.
when: When something was staged too early or into the wrong commit.
why: It changes the index without discarding work.

what: Show compact status with branch information.
when: Before deciding what to stage, commit, or push.
why: It shows branch and working-tree state without full prose.

when: When you only need the changed-path summary.
why: It is the quietest useful status view.

when: When compact status does not provide enough context.
why: It includes Git's explanations and suggested next commands.

when: Before staging or discarding working-tree edits.
why: It reviews what has changed but is not staged.

when: Immediately before committing.
why: It reviews exactly what the next commit will contain.

when: When inspecting or changing local branch metadata.
why: It is the direct entry point to git branch.

when: When locating work that is not visible locally.
why: It provides the complete branch overview.

when: When moving to existing work.
why: It uses the purpose-built switch command instead of checkout.

what: Create and switch to a branch.
when: When starting a new line of work.
why: It performs creation and switching atomically.

what: Show a commit or Git object.
when: When inspecting one specific revision.
why: It includes commit metadata and its patch.

what: Show decorated one-line history from HEAD.
when: When scanning recent commits quickly.
why: It keeps commit identity, subject, and refs on one line.

what: Show a decorated one-line graph from HEAD.
when: When understanding merges in current history.
why: The graph exposes branch topology without verbose patches.

what: Show the decorated graph across all refs.
when: When locating commits across branches and remotes.
why: It reveals relationships that HEAD-only history omits.

when: When reviewing the scope of recent commits.
why: It connects each commit to the files it touched.

what: Show history with statistics and full patches.
when: When a commit-by-commit code review needs full detail.
why: It combines history, file scope, and exact changes.

what: Create a commit with the staged diff visible in the editor.
when: When writing a considered commit message.
why: The staged diff provides context while composing the message.

what: Create a commit with a supplied message.
when: When the message is already clear and short.
why: It avoids opening an editor.

what: Create a fixup commit targeting another commit.
when: When correcting an earlier local commit before autosquash.
why: It records the intended squash target automatically.

when: When replaying local work onto a new base.
why: It keeps linear history when that is the chosen workflow.

when: When reordering, squashing, editing, or dropping commits.
why: It gives precise control over local history.

when: When the current conflict resolution path is wrong.
why: It returns to the state from before the rebase.

when: After resolving and staging current conflicts.
why: It resumes the paused rebase sequence.

when: When refreshing remote-tracking state.
why: It updates remote knowledge without changing local work.

what: Fetch all remotes and tags, pruning stale refs in parallel.
when: When refreshing the repository's complete remote view.
why: It cleans stale refs and speeds multi-remote fetching.

when: When updating a branch without adding a merge commit.
why: It replays local work on top of the fetched upstream.

when: When publishing commits to the current upstream.
why: It uses Git's configured push behavior without extra assumptions.

when: When work must be set aside temporarily.
why: It clears tracked edits while preserving them for later.

what: Apply and remove the latest stash.
when: When resuming the most recently stashed work.
why: It restores the changes and cleans up the stash entry.

when: When choosing which saved work to restore or inspect.
why: It shows stash identifiers and their descriptions.

what: Show the latest stash as a patch.
when: Before applying or dropping stashed work.
why: It reveals the exact saved changes.

what: Apply an existing commit to the current branch.
when: When reusing one focused commit without merging its branch.
why: It transfers the selected change and records a new commit.

when: When conflicts make the selected change unsuitable.
why: It returns to the state before the cherry-pick began.

when: After resolving and staging cherry-pick conflicts.
why: It completes the paused operation.
